They had sent these representatives to Adrian, who had been chosen to arbitrate. Throughout their journey from Paris to Calais, through empty towns and desolate countryside, the men had nursed a fierce hatred of one another. Now they argued their respective cases with undiminished partisan hostility.

By questioning the representatives separately and investigating at length, we discovered the true situation in Paris. Since Parliament had appointed Adrian as Ryland’s deputy, every surviving English person had accepted his authority. He was our captain, charged with leading us from our native country into unknown lands, our lawgiver and our protector. When we first organized our emigration, we had not intended any prolonged separation among our people. The whole chain of command rose by degrees to its highest point in the Earl of Windsor. Unforeseen circumstances, however, altered our plans, separating most of our people from their supreme leader for almost two months. They had crossed over in two distinct groups, and on reaching Paris they began to quarrel.

They had found Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, returning travelers and merchants, together with letters, brought us regular reports of the disease’s devastation on the continent. As the deaths increased, these exchanges dwindled and finally stopped. Even within England, communication between different parts of the island became slow and infrequent. No ship crossed the waters between Calais and Dover. Occasionally some sorrowful traveler would set out from the French coast, hoping to discover whether relatives among us were alive or dead; but often the hungry sea swallowed the little vessel. Others caught the disease a day or two after arriving and died before they could describe France’s desolation. We therefore knew very little about conditions on the continent and still held a vague hope of finding many companions across its broad expanse. But the forces that had so terribly reduced England’s population had found even greater scope for destruction in its neighboring country. France was empty. Along the entire road from Calais to Paris, not one human being had been encountered. Paris itself held a few, perhaps a hundred, who had accepted their approaching fate. They drifted through the capital’s streets and gathered to talk about earlier days with the animation, and even cheerfulness, that seldom abandons people of this nation.

The English occupied Paris without opposition. Its tall houses and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures could be seen at the familiar gathering place in the Tuileries. They wondered why the islanders would come to their doomed city. People in the depths of misery always imagine that their own portion of a disaster is the most bitter, just as, when suffering intense physical pain, we would trade the particular agony tormenting us for any other that might strike a different part of the body.

“Basil, this is extraordinary! I have to meet Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose from the seat and paced the garden. Eventually he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is simply an artistic inspiration to me. You might find nothing in him. I find everything. His presence in my work is strongest when his image doesn’t appear in it at all. As I said, he suggests a new style. I find him in the curves of particular lines, in the beauty and subtleties of particular colors. That’s all.”

“Then why won’t you exhibit his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because I’ve unintentionally expressed some of this strange artistic worship in it. Naturally, I’ve never wanted to speak to him about that. He knows nothing of it, and he never will. But the public might guess, and I refuse to expose my soul to their shallow, inquisitive eyes. I won’t let them put my heart under a microscope. There’s too much of me in that painting, Harry—too much of me!”

“Poets have fewer scruples. They understand how useful passion can be when you’re publishing. These days, a broken heart can sell through any number of editions.”

“I hate them for it,” Hallward exclaimed. “An artist ought to make beautiful things without putting any of his own life into them. We live at a time when people treat art as though it were supposed to be autobiography. We’ve lost our sense of beauty in the abstract. One day I’ll show the world what that means, and for that reason the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you’re mistaken, Basil, but I won’t argue. Only the intellectually lost ever argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter thought for a few moments. “He likes me,” he said at last. “I know he does. Of course, I flatter him outrageously. There’s a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I’ll regret afterward. Usually he’s charming with me, and we sit in the studio talking about a thousand different things. Sometimes, though, he’s terribly thoughtless and seems to take real pleasure in hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I’ve handed over my entire soul to someone who treats it like a flower for his lapel, a little decoration to please his vanity, an ornament to wear on a summer day.”

“April 19th. At about nine this morning, to my great joy, the pump of my air condenser finally showed clear signs of a change in the atmosphere. The moon’s surface was frighteningly close by then, and I was extremely alarmed. By ten I had reason to think the air had grown considerably denser. By eleven the apparatus needed very little effort to operate. At noon, after some hesitation, I dared to loosen the clamp. Feeling no discomfort, I eventually opened the rubber enclosure completely and removed it from around the basket. As might have been expected, this hasty and dangerous experiment immediately brought on spasms and a severe headache. But these symptoms, along with other breathing difficulties, were nowhere near serious enough to threaten my life. I decided to endure them as best I could, since I would soon escape them as I approached the denser layers of air near the moon. Yet I was still approaching at an extremely violent speed. It soon became alarmingly clear that, although I had probably been right to expect an atmosphere whose density matched the moon’s mass, I had wrongly assumed that even at the surface it would be dense enough to support the heavy load in my balloon’s basket. Yet it ought to have supported that weight as well as the earth’s atmosphere did, assuming that gravity on each world was proportional to the density of its air. My headlong fall was proof enough that this was not so. The only explanation must lie in the possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. Whatever the reason, I was now very close to the moon and descending with terrifying speed. Without wasting a moment, I threw out my ballast, then my water barrels, then the air condenser and rubber enclosure, and finally every other object in the basket. None of it helped. I was still falling horribly fast and was now no more than half a mile above the surface. As a last resort, I took off my coat, hat, and boots, then cut the basket itself free from the balloon, since it was quite heavy. Clinging to the netting with both hands, I had just enough time to see that the whole landscape, as far as I could look, was dotted thickly with tiny dwellings. Then I fell headfirst into the very center of a fantastically strange city, landing in the middle of a huge crowd of ugly little people. Not one of them said a word or made the slightest effort to help me. They simply stood there like a collection of idiots, grinning ridiculously and looking sideways at me and my balloon, with their hands planted on their hips.
